opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and least appreciated points. People often look at a large language model and ask, "Can it make a scientific discovery on its own?" And if you just prompt it once and take the answer, the honest response is usually no. These models hallucinate. They produce things that look plausible but are wrong. In most settings that's a bug. In FunSearch, we turned it into a feature.

The key idea is that the language model isn't working alone. It sits inside a harness, essentially an evolutionary loop. The model proposes programs, not final answers but code that solves a problem. Then an automated evaluator runs those programs and scores them objectively. The best ones go back into the prompt as examples, the model proposes variations, and you repeat this many times. So the model supplies creativity and diversity, and the evaluator supplies rigor. You get the imagination without being exposed to the hallucinations, because anything that's wrong simply gets filtered out.

That's why we focused on problems that are easy to verify but hard to solve. The cap set problem in combinatorics is a good example. If someone hands you a construction, checking it is straightforward, but finding a large one is extremely hard. With that setup, FunSearch found constructions that went beyond what was previously known, and that was a genuine new result in mathematics, not something sitting in the training data.

Searching over programs rather than raw solutions also matters a lot. A program is compact and interpretable. A mathematician can read it and say, "Oh, there's a symmetry being exploited here," and that insight can feed back into human understanding. The same applied to more practical problems like bin packing, where we found heuristics that beat standard approaches and could actually be inspected and deployed.

So the broader lesson I take is that the frontier of AI for science isn't only about bigger models. It's about the system around the model: how you generate candidates, how you verify them, how you maintain diversity so you don't collapse onto one idea, and how you keep humans in the loop to interpret what comes out. The language model is a powerful engine, but the harness is what turns it into a discovery machine.

r001.rationale: The response says an automated evaluator runs and objectively scores generated programs, filtering out incorrect ones and retaining stronger candidates.

r002.rationale: It calls hallucination a feature, but then says wrong outputs are filtered and discovery comes from the model’s creativity and diversity. It does not clearly state that apparent hallucinations themselves can produce novel scientific insights.

r003.rationale: The response attributes discovery to a system coupling the language model with an evaluator and an iterative evolutionary search loop.

fable-5.1.text:
The harness is really the whole point, in a sense. If you take a large language model on its own and ask it for a new mathematical construction, it will give you something plausible-sounding, and most of the time it will be wrong, or it will be something that's already in the literature. The model is a very good generator of ideas, but it has no reliable way of knowing which of those ideas are actually correct or actually new. So what FunSearch did was pair the model with something that does know: an evaluator, a piece of code that can score a candidate solution exactly.

That changes the nature of the problem. Instead of asking the model to be right, you ask it to propose. You have it write programs, not answers. A program that constructs a cap set, say, or a program that decides how to pack items into bins. Then you run that program, you score it against the ground truth, and the score is unambiguous. There's no hallucination possible at that stage, because either the construction has the size it claims or it doesn't.

The second piece is the evolutionary loop around that. You keep a population of the programs that scored well, you show the model a few of them, and you ask it to produce a variation. Most variations are no better. Occasionally one is, and it goes back into the pool. You do this hundreds of thousands, millions of times. The individual step is quite modest, but the aggregate search ends up exploring a space that no human would have the patience to explore by hand.

And I'd emphasise the choice of programs over raw solutions, because that was the part that surprised people. When FunSearch found the new cap set construction, we didn't just get a large set of points. We got a short program that generates it, and mathematicians could read that program and understand the structure. It gave them something to reason about. That's quite different from a black box producing a number.

So when I think about the harness, I think of it as three things: a verifier that cannot be fooled, a memory of what has worked so far, and a loop that turns a creative but unreliable model into a reliable search process. The model supplies intuition. The harness supplies rigour. Neither one alone gets you to a result that a mathematician would accept, and together they did.

r001.rationale: The response says the evaluator scores each generated program exactly and distinguishes valid, useful candidates from incorrect ones.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as an unreliable idea generator and says occasional variations improve, but does not say hallucinations can yield genuinely novel scientific insights.

r003.rationale: It attributes discovery to pairing the model with an exact evaluator and an evolutionary loop that repeatedly searches program variations.

astra-6.text:
I think the harness is absolutely central. In FunSearch, the language model proposes programs that might solve a problem, and then we execute those programs and evaluate how well they actually work. That gives us a feedback loop: we take the strongest candidates and use them to guide the model toward better ones.

The important distinction is that the model isn’t responsible for deciding whether its own idea is correct. It can be creative, it can propose something unexpected, and it can be wrong. The evaluator provides a check against the actual problem. Of course, that means you need a problem where you can reliably evaluate the proposals.

So the discovery comes from the whole system: the model generating possibilities, the evaluator testing them, and the search process building on what works. And because the output is a program, researchers can inspect it and try to understand the idea behind the improvement. That’s a very useful bridge between finding a better answer and gaining scientific insight.

r001.rationale: The response says the evaluator tests proposals against the actual problem, checks whether they work, and lets the search build on the strongest candidates. That communicates distinguishing failed ideas from valuable ones.

r002.rationale: It describes proposals as potentially unexpected and wrong, but does not say that apparent hallucinations can produce genuinely novel scientific insights.

r003.rationale: It attributes discovery to the combined system: the model generates possibilities, the evaluator tests them, and the search process builds on what works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the harness is absolutely critical. In FunSearch, the language model proposes programs, but we don’t ask the model itself to decide whether those programs represent a good discovery. We execute them and evaluate them against a precise objective. That gives us a feedback signal grounded in the problem, rather than in how convincing the model’s answer sounds.

The system then takes promising programs and feeds them back to the model, which generates new variations. So you have this iterative loop of proposing, testing, and improving. The model brings the ability to generate interesting ideas; the evaluator provides the discipline to distinguish ideas that actually work.

That’s an important way to think about scientific discovery with these models. It isn’t just about making the model bigger or asking it a clever question. It’s also about building an environment in which its suggestions can be tested reliably, and where the results of those tests guide the next round of exploration.

r002.rationale: It does not say that apparent hallucinations can lead to novel scientific insights.
